nance in a 24 h period). Add maintenance requirements plus replacement requirements for losses (vomiting, urine, etc.). A rough
guide for adults is 200–400 mL for every loose stool, for children 200 mL per motion, and for infants 1–1.5 times the usual feed. If
the patient is eating, calculate ﬂuid replacement at 75% of total. If the patient is diagnosed with hypotonic or isotonic dehydration,
calculate total ﬂuids (maintenance plus replacement) for the ﬁrst 24 h, and give half this amount over the next 8 h, and the other
half over the next 16 h. In hypertonic dehydration, correct the ﬂuid deﬁcits slowly over 48 h (Holliday and Segar, 1957).
In most instances involving heavy sweating, plain water containing 1.25 g of NaCl L1 is a suitable rehydration solution.
Increasing the concentration of NaCl to 5 or 6 g L1 may promote the rate of rehydration but may not be palatable for some indi-
viduals. Most commercial sports drinks contain 1.2–1.8 g NaCl L1 and are also good rehydration solutions, especially when both
ﬂuid and electrolytes have been lost through sweating. Fruit juices can also provide ﬂuid, energy, and electrolytes (e.g., fresh orange
juice contains approximately 10 mg of sodium and 2000 mg of potassium L) but may be too concentrated and delay gastric
